title: Veneto's CNG Gap: Why Metano Now Costs 15% More Here Than the Rest of Italy
dek: Petrol and diesel are tracking the national average almost exactly, but Veneto's natural-gas drivers are paying the widest regional premium tracked since July.
executive_summary: As of November 18 (the latest day in the feed), Veneto drivers pay €1.966/L for self-service Benzina, €2.229/L for Gasolio, €0.848/L for GPL, and €2.440/L for Metano. Three of those four numbers sit within a couple of cents of the national average — Benzina is effectively identical to the €1.966/L national figure, and Gasolio is a shade below the €2.233/L national average. 1,823 of Veneto's 1,982 registered stations reported a price that day, a 92.0% reporting rate, slightly ahead of the 90.4% national rate.

The outlier is Metano. Veneto's natural-gas price is €0.325/L above the €2.115/L national average — a 15.4% premium — and that gap hasn't appeared overnight. Back in the week of July 20, when this tracking series began, Veneto's Metano ran just 3.5% above the national price. That premium has since more than quadrupled, climbing through the high single digits over September and October before roughly doubling again to the mid-teens by early November, where it has now held for three straight weeks — the widest Veneto-vs-Italy gap for any fuel tracked since the data series started on July 21.

fuel_sections.heading: Petrol Holds Steady, Right on the National Line
paragraphs: Veneto's self-service Benzina priced at €1.9661/L on November 18, down 0.4% (-€0.0083) from €1.9744/L two days earlier. That's essentially identical to the national self-service average the same day, €1.9657/L — a gap of just €0.0004, or 0.02%.

Zoomed out, Veneto's Benzina has barely moved net across the 17 tracked weeks: €1.9725/L in the week of July 20 to €1.9703/L in the week of November 16, a drop of 0.1%. Nationally the fuel fell slightly more over the same stretch, -0.3% (from €1.9756/L to €1.9692/L). Both region and country rode the same run-up to a September peak — Veneto topped €2.1671/L in the week of September 21 — before easing back about 9% into November, moving in near-lockstep with the rest of the country throughout.

fuel_sections.heading: Diesel Cools From Its September Peak, Tracking the National Pace Almost Exactly
paragraphs: Veneto's self-service Gasolio priced at €2.2294/L on November 18, down 0.15% (-€0.0034) from €2.2328/L two days earlier. That's €0.0034 below the national self-service average the same day, €2.2328/L — a 0.15% discount, essentially at parity.

Over the full tracked window, Veneto's Gasolio climbed from €2.1705/L in the week of July 20 to €2.2311/L in the week of November 16, up 2.8%. Nationally it rose by almost exactly the same amount — 2.8%, from €2.1747/L to €2.2347/L. Both peaked in the week of September 21 (Veneto hit €2.3681/L) before easing roughly 5.8-5.9% into mid-November, a decline that has moved in step with Benzina's post-peak pullback.

fuel_sections.heading: LPG Keeps Climbing — and Veneto Is Outpacing the Rest of the Country
paragraphs: Veneto's self-service GPL priced at €0.8479/L on November 18, down slightly (-€0.0011, -0.1%) from €0.8490/L two days earlier. That's €0.0184 above the national self-service average the same day, €0.8295/L — a 2.2% regional premium.

The more telling number is the slope: Veneto's GPL has risen from €0.7631/L in the week of July 20 to €0.8484/L in the week of November 16, an 11.2% climb, outpacing the national rise of 9.1% (€0.7592/L to €0.8286/L) over the same 17 tracked weeks. The gap has widened gradually rather than in a single jump, and GPL is now the second-fastest-rising fuel in Veneto this autumn, behind only Metano.

fuel_sections.heading: The Real Story: Veneto's CNG Premium Has Quadrupled Since July
paragraphs: Veneto's self-service Metano (natural gas for cars) priced at €2.4396/L on November 18, down 1.0% (-€0.025) from €2.4646/L two days earlier — but that small dip barely registers next to the gap with the rest of the country. The national self-service average the same day was €2.1146/L, meaning Veneto drivers are paying €0.325/L more: a 15.4% premium.

That premium has widened steadily since tracking began. In the week of July 20, Veneto's Metano averaged €1.5527/L against a national €1.4999/L — just a 3.5% premium. By the week of November 16, Veneto's price had climbed to €2.4521/L (+57.9% since July) while the national average rose to only €2.1142/L (+41.0% over the same stretch). The regional premium held in the high single digits through most of September and October (8.5% as of the week of October 12), then roughly doubled to around 16% by early November and has stayed there for three straight weeks — the widest Veneto-vs-Italy gap for any of the four fuels tracked since this data series started on July 21.

network_section.heading: 92% of Veneto's Stations Reported Today — Above the National Average
paragraphs: Veneto has 1,982 registered fuel stations in the MIMIT registry, of which 1,823 reported a price on November 18 — a 92.0% reporting rate. Nationally, 21,660 of 23,958 registered stations reported that day, a 90.4% rate. Veneto's network is reporting slightly more consistently than the national average, a sign the region's price feed is unusually complete day to day.

Veneto's registered count has drifted down slightly over the tracked period, from 1,995 in July to 1,982 today — a net loss of 13 stations, or 0.7% — while the reporting count has stayed roughly flat in absolute terms. That points to the shrinkage being mostly network consolidation (station closures or re-registrations) rather than stations going dark on reporting.

methodology_section.heading: Built and Run by an Unattended Pipeline, Not a Spreadsheet
paragraphs: Every part of this report — the daily pull from MIMIT's official price feed, the national and regional averages across all 20 Italian regions and four fuel types, the day's region pick on a fixed rotation, the weekly trend analysis, and the write-up itself — is generated automatically, once a day, with no person in the loop. It was built with Claude Code, an AI coding agent, which wrote and now runs the data pipeline, the report template, and the analysis logic end to end.

Contrast that with how this kind of tracking usually gets done: a manually maintained spreadsheet, updated when someone remembers to open it, with figures that go stale the week nobody has time to refresh them. This pipeline doesn't have that failure mode by design — it runs the same checks every day whether or not anyone is watching.

closing.heading: Explore Further
paragraphs: The live dashboard opens on Agip Eni's brand-level view by default — use the scope picker to switch to Region, Province, Municipality, or another Operator/Brand and dig into any of Italy's 20 regions, hundreds of provinces and municipalities, or hundreds of tracked fuel brands.

pull_quote: Veneto's Metano premium over the rest of Italy has gone from 3.5% in July to roughly 16% today — the widest gap for any fuel tracked since the data series began.
caption:
Today's Fuel Dashboard spotlight: Veneto. The headline isn't the daily price moves — Benzina and Gasolio are both tracking the national average almost exactly, easing gently from their September peaks. It's Metano, natural gas for cars: Veneto drivers are now paying 15.4% more than the rest of Italy for it, up from just a 3.5% premium back in late July. That gap has roughly doubled since mid-October and is now the widest spread for any fuel tracked since this project started recording data on July 21.

Fuel Dashboard tracks self-service and served prices for Benzina, Gasolio, GPL and Metano across every Italian region, province, municipality and fuel brand, pulling Italy's official MIMIT price feed every morning — no spreadsheet, no manual refresh. Take a look: https://adeo-blip.github.io/fuel-price-italy/

I built this entirely with Claude Code: the data pull, the regional rotation, the weekly trend analysis, and even this write-up all run unattended, once a day. It's a concrete case for letting an AI agent own a tracking pipeline end to end instead of defaulting to "put it in Excel" — faster to build, and it keeps updating even on the days nobody has time to touch it.
